article_title: How to Report a Fraudulent UPI Transaction and Actually Get Your Money Back
claim: RBI's guidelines on limited customer liability apply differently depending on the situation — banks often treat a self-authorized (tricked) transaction differently from one you never approved at all, since UPI payments are PIN-authenticated from the bank's view.
source: RBI — Customer Protection: Limited Liability of Customers in Unauthorised Electronic Banking Transactions, DBR.No.Leg.BC.78/09.07.005/2017-18, dated 6 July 2017
required_correction: This is the single biggest gap flagged by the editorial review: the article describes RBI liability rules only in vague, qualitative terms and never states the actual tiers readers need. The real framework: Zero Liability if the fraud stems from bank negligence/system breach and unrelated to customer, or if reported within 3 working days of notification; Limited Liability (capped at ₹5,000 for basic savings accounts, ₹10,000 for other savings accounts/prepaid instruments, ₹25,000 for credit cards with limits above ₹5 lakh) for reporting within 4–7 working days; beyond 7 working days, liability follows the bank's own Board-approved policy. Banks must credit the disputed amount within 10 working days of notification. The article's framing that a self-authorized/tricked transaction is simply 'treated differently' understates that scam victims who were tricked into authorizing (OTP/UPI PIN entry) can still fall under zero/limited liability if they report within these specific windows — the current vague text risks readers concluding they have no protection once they 'technically authorized' the payment, which is not accurate. Add the actual tiers and timeframes with a citation to this RBI circular.
